comp.label: A Thousand Lodgers
comp.compStory:
If you want to see a city, you do not need to travel to London or New York. You only need to find an old oak tree and sit underneath it for an hour.

At first, you will see very little: a trunk, some branches, a scatter of leaves. Oaks are not showy trees. They do not flower in clouds of pink like cherries, or blaze red in autumn like maples. An oak simply stands there, broad and grey and patient, as though it has been waiting for you to notice it, and is prepared to wait a good deal longer.

But look closer, and the city begins to appear.

Start at the bottom. Among the roots, hidden in the soil, runs a web of fungus threads so fine that a single one is almost invisible. Together they spread for metres, wrapping around the roots like a glove. The fungus helps the tree to drink in water and minerals; in return, the tree feeds the fungus with sugar made in its leaves. Neither could thrive so well alone. It is a partnership older than any human city, and far better run.

Now look at the bark. What you took for grey is really a patchwork of pale green, yellow and silver: lichens, each one a partnership of its own, clinging to the ridges. In the cracks between them live beetles, spiders and tiny insects that most of us would never see without a magnifying glass. A treecreeper, a small brown bird with a curved beak, spirals up the trunk, picking them out one by one like a shopper working along the shelves.

Higher still, the branches are busy. Caterpillars chew the young leaves in spring, and blue tits time the hatching of their chicks so that there are as many caterpillars as possible to feed them. Woodpeckers drill holes that, years later, become homes for owls or roosting places for bats. Squirrels build untidy nests called dreys where the branches fork. Scientists who studied Britain's native oaks found that more than two thousand different species make use of them in some way. Some could live almost nowhere else.

Even the oak's leaves, when they fall, are not wasted. They are tough and slow to rot, so they form a thick blanket on the ground, sheltering worms, woodlice and the creatures that feed on them. Slowly, they break down and return their goodness to the soil, which feeds the roots, which feed the tree. Nothing in this city is thrown away.

Then there are the acorns. In a good year, a single large oak may drop tens of thousands of them. Most are eaten by mice, deer, pigeons or wild boar. But the jay, a bird with a pinkish body and a flash of electric blue on its wings, does something cleverer. It carries acorns away and buries them, one at a time, to eat in winter. A jay can bury thousands in a single autumn, and it does not find them all. The ones it forgets may become new oaks, perhaps hundreds of metres from their parent. Without meaning to, the jay is a gardener.

All of this takes time. An oak may not produce acorns until it is forty years old, and it may live for many hundreds of years. Some of the oaks standing in Britain today were already old when the first steam trains ran. They have watched over fields and villages that have changed beyond recognition, while they themselves have changed only slowly.

This is perhaps the most important thing an oak can teach us. We live in a hurry. We expect answers in seconds and parcels by tomorrow. An oak works on a different clock. The person who plants an acorn will almost certainly never sit in the shade of the tree it becomes. They plant it anyway, for people they will never meet.

So the next time you pass an old oak, slow down. Sit for a while. Watch the treecreeper on its spiral and the jay on its errands. Listen to the leaves. You are not looking at one tree. You are looking at a city of a thousand lodgers, built without a single brick, that has been quietly working for longer than anyone can remember.

And if you happen to find an acorn, you might consider planting it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer begin by comparing an oak tree to a city?
questions.optionA: To show that oak trees grow best in cities
questions.optionB: To compare the size of an oak with a skyscraper
questions.optionC: To suggest that an oak is home to a huge number of living things that depend on each other
questions.optionD: To persuade readers to visit London or New York
questions.optionE: To explain that cities are bad for trees
questions.explanation: The whole article shows the oak as a busy, crowded home where many creatures live and work together.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to the article, which of these is NOT true of oaks?
questions.optionA: They can live for many hundreds of years
questions.optionC: They have tough leaves that are slow to rot
questions.optionE: They are used by more than two thousand species
questions.explanation: The writer says oaks do NOT 'blaze red in autumn like maples'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The oak "is prepared to wait a good deal longer". What does this personification suggest?
questions.optionB: That the oak is about to fall down
questions.optionC: That the oak is calm and in no hurry
questions.optionD: That the oak is angry at being ignored
questions.optionE: That the oak is waiting for rain
questions.explanation: Giving the tree human patience prepares for the later idea that an oak 'works on a different clock'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What does the tree give the fungus in return for help with water and minerals?
questions.optionC: Shelter from the rain
questions.optionE: Sugar made in its leaves
questions.explanation: 'The tree feeds the fungus with sugar made in its leaves.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The fungus wraps around the roots "like a glove". What does this simile suggest?
questions.optionB: It can easily be taken off
questions.optionC: It keeps the roots warm in winter
questions.optionD: It protects the roots from animals
questions.optionE: It fits closely all around the roots
questions.explanation: A glove fits snugly around a hand, just as the fungus threads wrap tightly around the roots.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer say the partnership is "far better run" than a human city?
questions.optionA: Because it has a mayor and a council
questions.optionC: Because both partners benefit and nothing is wasted
questions.optionD: Because fungi are cleverer than people
questions.optionE: Because it is much smaller than a city
questions.explanation: Each side gives the other what it needs, a fairness the writer suggests human cities do not always manage.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: In the article, what does "thrive" mean?
questions.optionC: Survive with difficulty
questions.optionE: Move away
questions.explanation: 'Neither could thrive so well alone' means neither would grow and do as well on its own.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: The treecreeper picks out insects "like a shopper working along the shelves". What does this suggest about how it feeds?
questions.optionA: It shares its food with other birds
questions.optionB: It searches carefully and steadily, choosing food as it goes
questions.optionC: It feeds very quickly and carelessly
questions.optionD: It feeds on the shelves of fungus
questions.optionE: It feeds only on food bought from shops
questions.explanation: A shopper moves along methodically, picking items one by one, as the bird does on the trunk.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why do blue tits time the hatching of their chicks?
questions.optionA: So that there is as much food as possible when the chicks need feeding
questions.optionB: So that they can use the squirrels' dreys
questions.optionC: So that the chicks hatch before the woodpeckers
questions.optionD: So that the chicks can leave before winter
questions.optionE: So that the caterpillars do not eat the eggs
questions.explanation: They hatch when there are 'as many caterpillars as possible to feed them'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is a drey?
questions.optionC: A hole made by a woodpecker
questions.optionE: A bat's roosting place
questions.explanation: 'Squirrels build untidy nests called dreys.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: How do woodpeckers help other animals, according to the article?
questions.optionA: The holes they drill later become homes for owls and bats
questions.optionB: They warn other birds of danger
questions.optionC: They eat the caterpillars that damage leaves
questions.optionD: They bury acorns that grow into new trees
questions.optionE: They keep the bark free of lichen
questions.explanation: Holes drilled by woodpeckers 'years later, become homes for owls or roosting places for bats'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: "Nothing in this city is thrown away." How does this sentence connect to the paragraph before it?
questions.optionA: It explains why oaks lose their leaves
questions.optionB: It contradicts what the writer said about leaves
questions.optionC: It shows the writer is worried about litter
questions.optionD: It sums up how fallen leaves are recycled back into the soil to feed the tree
questions.optionE: It introduces a new paragraph about acorns
questions.explanation: The paragraph traces leaves to soil to roots to tree; the closing sentence sums up the cycle.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the writer call the jay "a gardener"?
questions.optionA: Because it eats insects that harm plants
questions.optionB: Because by forgetting buried acorns it plants new oaks
questions.optionC: Because it digs up worms
questions.optionE: Because it lives in gardens
questions.explanation: The jay buries acorns and does not find them all, so it plants trees 'without meaning to'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: According to the article, how old may an oak be before it produces acorns?
questions.optionC: Ten years old
questions.optionE: One hundred years old
questions.explanation: 'An oak may not produce acorns until it is forty years old.'

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What does the writer suggest is "the most important thing an oak can teach us"?
questions.optionA: To be patient and to do things that will benefit others in the future
questions.optionB: To travel less and stay at home
questions.optionC: To protect the animals that live in oaks
questions.optionE: To plant as many trees as possible
questions.explanation: We 'live in a hurry', but someone who plants an acorn does it 'for people they will never meet'.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why do several paragraphs begin with phrases such as "Start at the bottom", "Now look at the bark" and "Higher still"?
questions.optionA: They give instructions for climbing a tree
questions.optionB: They guide the reader up the tree, as if on a tour
questions.optionC: They show the order in which the tree grows
questions.optionD: They show that the writer is lost
questions.optionE: They list the parts of a tree in alphabetical order
questions.explanation: The phrases move the reader from roots to bark to branches, like a guide leading a tour.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: What is the main purpose of the article?
questions.optionA: To compare oaks with every other kind of tree
questions.optionB: To help readers appreciate how much life an oak supports and why it is worth valuing
questions.optionC: To describe the life of a jay
questions.optionD: To argue that oaks should be cut down
questions.optionE: To explain how to grow an oak from an acorn
questions.explanation: The article reveals the oak's hidden 'city' and ends by encouraging readers to slow down and value it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH
questions.quest: Why does the article end with the suggestion that you might plant an acorn?
questions.optionA: It reminds readers that jays bury acorns
questions.optionB: It invites the reader to act on the lesson about patience and the future
questions.optionC: It warns readers not to eat acorns
questions.optionD: It shows that acorns are rare
questions.optionE: It suggests that the writer has run out of ideas
questions.explanation: Planting an acorn is exactly the patient, unselfish act the writer has just praised.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 647 × 38?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is 4/9 × 3/8?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: In a test, Maya scored 36 out of 48. What percentage is this?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A map has a scale of 1 : 25,000. Two villages are 6 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
questions.optionC: 1.5 km
questions.optionE: 25 km

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Which expression means "add 5 to n, then multiply by 3"?
questions.explanation: Adding first means the bracket comes first: (n + 5) × 3 = 3(n + 5).

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Which rule gives the nth term of the sequence 3, 7, 11, 15, …?
questions.explanation: It goes up by 4, so it starts 4n; 4 × 1 = 4 and the first term is 3, so subtract 1.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the range of 9, 4, 15, 7, 12, 7?
questions.explanation: Range = largest − smallest = 15 − 4 = 11. (7 is the mode.)

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A café sells sandwiches at £3 and cakes at £2. On Monday it sold 7 sandwiches and 4 cakes. How much money did it take?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: What is the size of each interior angle of a regular hexagon?
questions.explanation: The angles of a hexagon add to (6 − 2) × 180° = 720°; 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Find the angle marked x.

questions.explanation: Angles on a straight line add up to 180°: 180 − 47 = 133°.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A rectangular garden is 12 m long and has an area of 78 m². How wide is it?
questions.optionE: 7 m
questions.explanation: Width = area ÷ length = 78 ÷ 12 = 6.5 m.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A bag of flour weighs 3.45 kg. Tom uses 1,750 g. How much is left?
questions.optionE: 5.2 kg

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A flight leaves at 23:40 and lasts 1 hour 35 minutes. At what time does it land?
questions.explanation: 23:40 + 20 min = 00:00; another 1 h 15 min gives 01:15.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: How many square numbers are between 50 and 150?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: Which of these is 72 written as a product of prime factors?
questions.optionE: 2² × 3³

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest:
Which number is the third smallest?
0.405   0.45   0.4   0.425   0.44

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: The point (−2, 5) is moved 4 units right and 3 units down. Where does it end up?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A fair dice is rolled 120 times. About how many times would you expect it to land on 6?
questions.explanation: The chance of a 6 is 1/6; 1/6 of 120 is 20.

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A pencil costs p pence and a ruler costs 13p more. Three pencils and a ruler cost 85p. How much is one pencil?

questions.subject: MATHS
questions.quest: A cyclist rides at 18 km/h. How far does she ride in 40 minutes?
questions.optionC: 720 km
questions.optionE: 10 km
questions.explanation: 40 minutes is 2/3 of an hour; 2/3 × 18 = 12 km.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, MINT is written as NHOS. How would CLOUD be written in the same code?
questions.optionC: DKPTE
questions.optionE: BMNVC
questions.explanation: The letters move forward 1, back 1, forward 1, back 1, and so on: C→D, L→K, O→P, U→T, D→E.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: In a code, SHIP is written as KRSH. How would BOAT be written in the same code?
questions.optionC: GZLY
questions.optionE: GZLX
questions.explanation: Each letter is swapped with its partner from the other end of the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, …) and then the word is written backwards. BOAT → YLZG → GZLY.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next letter: Z, B, X, D, V, F, ?
questions.optionC: U
questions.optionE: H
questions.explanation: Two series take turns: Z, X, V, T go back 2 each time; B, D, F go forward 2.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 5, 7, 11, 19, 35, ?
questions.explanation: The differences double each time: 2, 4, 8, 16, so the next difference is 32: 35 + 32 = 67.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Find the next number: 100, 99, 96, 91, 84, ?
questions.explanation: The amounts taken away are 1, 3, 5, 7, so next is 9: 84 − 9 = 75.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
The numbers in each group are related in the same way. Find the missing number.
6 (24) 5     4 (28) 8     7 ( ? ) 6
questions.explanation: Multiply the outside numbers, then take away the first: 6 × 5 − 6 = 24, 4 × 8 − 4 = 28, 7 × 6 − 7 = 35.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three letters that make a word have been taken out of the word in capitals. Which three letters complete it?
A robin sat on the highest BCH of the tree.
questions.optionC: OAT
questions.optionE: END
questions.explanation: B + RAN + CH = BRANCH.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Find the word that completes the third pair in the same way as the first two.
(stop, pots)   (reed, deer)   (lever, ?)
questions.optionC: never
questions.optionE: level
questions.explanation: Each word is written backwards: stop → pots, reed → deer, lever → revel.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Choose one word from each group that are closest in meaning.
(ancient, polite, sudden)   (courteous, rude, gradual)
questions.optionC: sudden, gradual
questions.optionE: ancient, gradual
questions.explanation: Polite and courteous both mean having good manners. Polite/rude and sudden/gradual are opposites.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Choose one word from each group that are most nearly OPPOSITE in meaning.
(generous, hidden, swift)   (concealed, rapid, selfish)
questions.optionC: swift, selfish
questions.optionE: hidden, concealed
questions.explanation: Generous means happy to give; selfish means thinking only of yourself. Hidden/concealed and swift/rapid mean the same.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Three of these words go together. Which TWO do not belong?
square   circle   cube   triangle   sphere
questions.optionC: square, circle
questions.optionE: square, cube
questions.explanation: Square, circle and triangle are flat (2-D) shapes. Cubes and spheres are solid (3-D).

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
A five-letter word is hidden across the end of one word and the start of the next. Which pair hides it?
"The bear thought hard about the honey."
questions.optionC: hard about
questions.optionE: The bear
questions.explanation: b(EAR TH)ought hides EARTH.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: PM is to KH as WT is to ?
questions.optionC: QN
questions.optionE: SP
questions.explanation: Each letter moves back 5 places: P→K, M→H, so W→R and T→O.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: A clock loses 4 minutes every hour. It is set to the right time at 9:00 am. What time will it show when the real time is 3:00 pm the same day?
questions.explanation: From 9 am to 3 pm is 6 hours, so the clock loses 6 × 4 = 24 minutes and shows 2:36 pm.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: Ava is taller than Ben. Cal is shorter than Ben but taller than Dee. Eve is taller than Ava. Who is the third tallest?
questions.optionC: Eve
questions.optionE: Dee
questions.explanation: From tallest: Eve, Ava, Ben, Cal, Dee. Ben is third.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If A = 4, B = 6, C = 8, D = 12 and E = 24, what is (A × B) ÷ (C − A)? Give your answer as a letter.
questions.optionC: C
questions.optionE: E
questions.explanation: A × B = 24 and C − A = 4; 24 ÷ 4 = 6, which is B.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Everyone in the chess club also plays football. Some footballers wear glasses. Sam is in the chess club.
Which statement MUST be true?
questions.optionC: All footballers play chess
questions.optionE: Sam plays football
questions.explanation: Everyone in the chess club plays football, so Sam must. Nothing tells us whether Sam, or any chess player, wears glasses.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
The word in brackets is made from the two outside words. Make the missing word in the same way.
fish [shop] stop        rose [ ? ] boat
questions.optionC: seat
questions.optionE: sent
questions.explanation: The last two letters of the first word and the last two of the second: fi(SH) + st(OP) = SHOP, ro(SE) + bo(AT) = SEAT.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest:
Choose one word from each group to complete the sentence.
Pen is to (paper, write, ink) as knife is to (blade, cut, fork).
questions.optionC: ink, cut
questions.optionE: write, blade
questions.explanation: A pen is used to write; a knife is used to cut.

questions.subject: VERBAL
questions.quest: If A = 1, B = 2, C = 3 and so on up to Z = 26, which word has letters that add up to 20?
questions.optionC: CAGE
questions.optionE: BEAD
questions.explanation: J + A + D + E = 10 + 1 + 4 + 5 = 20. (BEAD 12, FACE 15, HIDE 26, CAGE 16.)
